question: The Mahatma Gandhi (New) Series of banknotes was introduced by the Reserve Bank of India in which year?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 2016.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Mahatma Gandhi (New) Series of banknotes was introduced by the Reserve Bank of India in November 2016, following the demonetisation of the old ₹500 and ₹1000 notes. (महात्मा गांधी नई शृंखला — 2016)

 

• The new series began with the ₹2000 and the redesigned ₹500 notes, and was followed by the ₹200, ₹100, ₹50, ₹20 and ₹10 denominations. Each note carries a motif of India's cultural heritage on the reverse — the Mangalyaan on the ₹2000, the Red Fort on the ₹500, Sanchi Stupa on the ₹200, Rani ki Vav on the ₹100, Hampi with Chariot on the ₹50 and Ellora Caves on the ₹20.

 

• The earlier Mahatma Gandhi Series had been launched in 1996, replacing the Ashoka Pillar series.

 

• In May 2023 the RBI announced the withdrawal of the ₹2000 note from circulation, though it remains legal tender.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Currency in India is issued by the RBI under Section 22 of the RBI Act, 1934, in denominations from ₹2 to ₹2000. The ₹1 note is issued by the Ministry of Finance and bears the signature of the Finance Secretary; all coins are also issued by the Government of India.

 

• Indian currency notes carry the denomination in 17 languages — Hindi and English on the front, and 15 other languages on the reverse language panel.

 

• Notes are printed at presses in Nashik, Dewas, Mysuru and Salboni, and coins are minted at Mumbai, Kolkata, Hyderabad and Noida.

 

NOTE

 

• 2010 (Option 1): The year the Indian Rupee symbol (₹), designed by D. Udaya Kumar, was adopted.

 

• 2014 (Option 2) and 2018 (Option 4): Neither year marks the introduction of the series; the ₹100 note of the new series was issued in 2018, but the series itself began in 2016.

question: Which ruler of Magadha shifted the capital from Rajgir (Girivraja) to Pataliputra?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Udayin.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Udayin, the son and successor of Ajatashatru, shifted the capital of Magadha from Rajgir (Girivraja) to Pataliputra, at the confluence of the Ganga and the Son. (उदयिन — राजगृह से पाटलिपुत्र)

 

• Pataliputra's position at the meeting of rivers made it both easy to defend and convenient for trade, and it remained the capital under the Nandas, Mauryas and Guptas.

 

• The early rulers of Magadha and their achievements:
◦ Bimbisara (544-492 BCE) — of the Haryanka dynasty; expanded Magadha by matrimonial alliances and by annexing Anga; a contemporary of both the Buddha and Mahavira.
◦ Ajatashatru (492-460 BCE) — annexed Kashi and Vaishali; used the war engines Rathamusala and Mahashilakantaka; the First Buddhist Council was held at Rajgir in his reign.
◦ Udayin — founded Pataliputra.
◦ Shishunaga — founded the Shishunaga dynasty and destroyed the power of Avanti.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Magadha's rise was helped by its fertile alluvial soil, the iron ore deposits near Rajgir, its command of the Ganga trade route, the use of elephants from the eastern forests, and a succession of able and ambitious rulers.

 

• The Nanda dynasty was founded by Mahapadma Nanda, called Ekarat and Sarvakshatrantaka; its last ruler, Dhana Nanda, was overthrown by Chandragupta Maurya with the help of Chanakya.

 

NOTE

 

• Bimbisara (Option 1): The real founder of Magadha's greatness, but his capital was Rajgir.

 

• Ajatashatru (Option 2): Fortified Rajgir and is said to have laid a fort at Pataligrama, but the transfer of the capital was made by his successor.

 

• Shishunaga (Option 4): Temporarily shifted the capital to Vaishali, not to Pataliputra.

question: In which language were the Buddhist Tripitakas originally composed?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Pali.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Tripitakas, the earliest and most sacred texts of Buddhism, were originally composed in Pali, the language of the common people of Magadha in the Buddha's time. (त्रिपिटक — पालि भाषा में)

 

• The three Pitakas ("baskets") are:
◦ Vinaya Pitaka — the rules of discipline for monks and nuns
◦ Sutta Pitaka — the discourses and sermons of the Buddha; it contains the Jataka stories
◦ Abhidhamma Pitaka — the philosophical and psychological analysis of the doctrine

 

• The Buddha deliberately preached in Pali rather than Sanskrit so that his teaching might be understood by ordinary people. Later Mahayana texts, however, were written in Sanskrit.

 

• The Tripitakas were finally written down at the Fourth Buddhist Council in Sri Lanka in the first century BCE.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Languages of the principal religious texts:
◦ Vedas, Upanishads, Puranas, Ramayana, Mahabharata — Sanskrit
◦ Buddhist Tripitakas — Pali
◦ Jain Agamas (Angas) — Ardhamagadhi Prakrit
◦ Ashokan edicts — Prakrit, in the Brahmi and Kharosthi scripts

 

• The four Buddhist Councils: the First at Rajgir under Ajatashatru; the Second at Vaishali under Kalasoka; the Third at Pataliputra under Ashoka, presided over by Moggaliputta Tissa; and the Fourth in Kashmir under Kanishka, at which Buddhism split into Hinayana and Mahayana.

 

NOTE

 

• Sanskrit (Option 1): The language of the Vedas and of later Mahayana Buddhist literature, but not of the original Tripitakas.

 

• Prakrit (Option 3): A family of vernacular languages, of which Pali is one; the answer required here is the specific one.

 

• Ardhamagadhi (Option 4): The Prakrit dialect in which the Jain canonical texts were composed.

question: A judge of the Supreme Court of India can be removed from office by the President only on an address by ______.
option_2: both Houses of Parliament, passed by a special majority
option_3: the Chief Justice of India and two senior-most judges
option_4: the Lok Sabha alone, passed by a simple majority
solution_text:
The correct answer is both Houses of Parliament, passed by a special majority.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Under Article 124(4), a judge of the Supreme Court may be removed from office by an order of the President, but only after an address by both Houses of Parliament has been presented to him in the same session. (न्यायाधीश को हटाने की प्रक्रिया — महाभियोग)

 

• The address must be supported in each House by:
◦ a majority of the total membership of that House, and
◦ a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting.

 

• The grounds are only two — proved misbehaviour or incapacity.

 

• The procedure is governed by the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968. A removal motion requires the signatures of 100 members of the Lok Sabha or 50 members of the Rajya Sabha, and is investigated by a three-member committee consisting of a Supreme Court judge, a Chief Justice of a High Court and a distinguished jurist.

 

• No judge of the Supreme Court has ever been removed by this process. The first attempt was against Justice V. Ramaswami in 1993, but the motion failed in the Lok Sabha.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The same procedure applies to the removal of a High Court judge (Article 217), the Comptroller and Auditor General (Article 148) and the Chief Election Commissioner (Article 324).

 

• The President is removed by impeachment under Article 61, for the violation of the Constitution, by a resolution passed in each House by a two-thirds majority of the total membership.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 is incorrect — the executive has no power to remove a judge, which is a central safeguard of judicial independence.

 

• Option 3 is incorrect — the collegium recommends appointments and transfers, but cannot remove a judge.

 

• Option 4 is incorrect — the address must come from both Houses, and by a special majority, not a simple one.

question: Which of the following connective tissues joins a muscle to a bone in the human body?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Tendon.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A tendon is the fibrous connective tissue that joins a muscle to a bone. (कंडरा — पेशी को अस्थि से जोड़ना)

 

• Tendons are made of white fibrous connective tissue, are very strong and inelastic, and transmit the pull of the muscle to the bone so that movement takes place. The Achilles tendon at the heel is the largest and strongest in the human body.

 

• The distinction to remember:
◦ Tendon — joins muscle to bone; strong and non-elastic
◦ Ligament — joins bone to bone; contains yellow elastic fibres and is very elastic, which allows joints to move

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The four principal types of animal tissue are epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous.

 

• Connective tissues include blood (a fluid connective tissue), bone, cartilage, tendon, ligament, areolar tissue and adipose tissue (which stores fat).

 

• Muscular tissue is of three kinds: striated (skeletal, voluntary), smooth (unstriated, involuntary) and cardiac, which is striated but involuntary and found only in the heart.

 

• The human body has 206 bones in the adult and 300 at birth. The femur is the longest bone and the stapes in the ear the smallest.

 

NOTE

 

• Ligament (Option 1): Joins bone to bone at a joint; a sprain is an injury to a ligament.

 

• Areolar tissue (Option 2): A loose packing tissue found between the skin and muscles and around blood vessels and nerves; it fills spaces and supports organs.

 

• Cartilage (Option 3): A soft, flexible connective tissue found at the ends of bones, in the nose, the ear and the trachea; it reduces friction at joints.

question:
Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding the Third Battle of Panipat (1761)?

I. It was fought between the Marathas and Ahmad Shah Abdali.

II. The Maratha forces were led by Sadashivrao Bhau.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both I and II.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both statements are correct. (पानीपत का तृतीय युद्ध, 1761 — मराठा बनाम अहमद शाह अब्दाली)

 

• Statement I is correct: the Third Battle of Panipat was fought on 14 January 1761 between the Marathas and Ahmad Shah Abdali (Ahmad Shah Durrani) of Afghanistan, who was supported by Najib-ud-Daula of Rohilkhand and Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh.

 

• Statement II is correct: the Maratha army was commanded by Sadashivrao Bhau, the cousin of Peshwa Balaji Baji Rao, with Vishwasrao, the Peshwa's son, as the nominal head. Ibrahim Khan Gardi commanded the Maratha artillery.

 

• The Marathas suffered a crushing defeat. Both Sadashivrao Bhau and Vishwasrao were killed, and the Peshwa Balaji Baji Rao died soon afterwards. The defeat halted Maratha expansion in the north for a decade and, by weakening the strongest Indian power, indirectly cleared the way for the East India Company.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The three battles of Panipat:
◦ First (1526) — Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi, founding the Mughal Empire; the first use of field artillery and the Tulughma tactic in India.
◦ Second (1556) — Akbar's forces under Bairam Khan defeated Hemu (Hemchandra Vikramaditya).
◦ Third (1761) — Ahmad Shah Abdali defeated the Marathas.

 

• Ahmad Shah Abdali invaded India several times between 1748 and 1767 and had earlier seized Punjab, Multan, Kashmir and Sindh from the Mughals.

 

NOTE

 

• Options 1, 2 and 4 are incorrect, because both the given statements are factually accurate.

question: What is the formula used to calculate the density of a substance?
option_4: Density = Mass x Volume x Volume
solution_text:
The correct answer is Density = Mass / Volume.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Density is defined as the mass per unit volume of a substance. (घनत्व = द्रव्यमान / आयतन)
◦ d = m / V
◦ Its SI unit is kg/m³; in the CGS system it is g/cm³. The two are related by 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³.
◦ Density is a scalar quantity.

 

• The density of pure water at 4°C is 1 g/cm³ or 1000 kg/m³, which is its maximum density. Water is unusual in that it expands on freezing, so that ice is less dense than water and therefore floats — a property called the anomalous expansion of water, and the reason why aquatic life survives in frozen lakes.

 

• Relative density (specific gravity) is the ratio of the density of a substance to that of water. It has no unit, being a ratio, and is measured by a hydrometer.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Related formulae frequently asked in SSC:
◦ Weight, W = m × g
◦ Pressure, P = F / A; pressure of a liquid column, P = hρg
◦ Speed = Distance / Time; Acceleration = (v − u) / t
◦ Force, F = m × a; Momentum, p = m × v
◦ Work, W = F × d; Power = Work / Time

 

• A lactometer measures the purity of milk, and a hydrometer the relative density of liquids; both work on the principle of flotation and Archimedes' Principle.

 

NOTE

 

• Options 1, 3 and 4 invert or misuse the relationship. Note in particular Option 3, in which volume is divided by mass — this gives the specific volume, the reciprocal of density, and is the commonest error in this question.

question: The Santhali language, included in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution, is written in which script?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ol Chiki.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Santhali is written in the Ol Chiki script, devised in 1925 by Pandit Raghunath Murmu. (संताली — ओल चिकी लिपि)

 

• Santhali belongs to the Munda branch of the Austroasiatic family of languages — one of the very few Austroasiatic languages in the Eighth Schedule. It is spoken chiefly in Jharkhand, West Bengal, Odisha, Bihar and Assam, and the Santhals are the largest tribal community of India.

 

• It was included in the Eighth Schedule by the 92nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003, along with Bodo, Dogri and Maithili.

 

• The Ol Chiki script has 30 letters and is written from left to right. Before its adoption Santhali had been written in the Bengali, Odia and Roman scripts.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Scripts of some scheduled languages: Devanagari — Hindi, Marathi, Nepali, Konkani, Sanskrit, Bodo, Dogri and Maithili; Meitei Mayek — Manipuri; Gurmukhi — Punjabi; Perso-Arabic — Urdu, Kashmiri and Sindhi; Ol Chiki — Santhali.

 

• India's four principal language families: Indo-Aryan (about 78% of speakers), Dravidian (about 20%), Austroasiatic (Munda) and Tibeto-Burman. Great Andamanese forms a separate family.

 

• The Eighth Schedule contains 22 languages. Hindi has the greatest number of speakers and Sanskrit the fewest.

 

NOTE

 

• Devanagari (Option 1): Used for Hindi, Marathi, Nepali and several other scheduled languages, but not for Santhali.

 

• Bengali (Option 3) and Odia (Option 4): Both were used for writing Santhali before the adoption of Ol Chiki, but neither is its recognised script today.

question: The Prarthana Samaj, a socio-religious reform movement, was founded in 1867 in which city?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bombay.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Prarthana Samaj was founded at Bombay in 1867 by Dr. Atmaram Pandurang, with the encouragement of Keshab Chandra Sen of the Brahmo Samaj during his visit to western India. (प्रार्थना समाज — बंबई, 1867)

 

• Its most distinguished members were Mahadev Govind Ranade, who became its guiding spirit, R.G. Bhandarkar and N.G. Chandavarkar.

 

• It worked for four social reforms: the abolition of caste distinctions, the abolition of child marriage, widow remarriage, and the education of women and the depressed classes. Unlike the Brahmo Samaj, it did not regard itself as a separate sect but as a movement of reform within Hinduism.

 

• Ranade also founded the Deccan Education Society and the Widow Remarriage Association, and was associated with the Indian National Social Conference.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Major socio-religious reform organisations and their founders:
◦ Brahmo Samaj (1828, Calcutta) — Raja Rammohan Roy
◦ Young Bengal Movement (1820s) — Henry Louis Vivian Derozio
◦ Arya Samaj (1875, Bombay) — Swami Dayanand Saraswati; slogan "Back to the Vedas"
◦ Ramakrishna Mission (1897) — Swami Vivekananda
◦ Theosophical Society (1875, New York; 1882 at Adyar) — Madame Blavatsky and Colonel Olcott
◦ Satyashodhak Samaj (1873, Poona) — Jyotiba Phule
◦ Aligarh Movement — Sir Syed Ahmad Khan
◦ Singh Sabha (1873, Amritsar) — a Sikh reform movement

 

NOTE

 

• Calcutta (Option 1): The birthplace of the Brahmo Samaj, whose ideas inspired the Prarthana Samaj.

 

• Poona (Option 3): The centre of the Satyashodhak Samaj and of Ranade's later educational work, but not the founding place of the Prarthana Samaj.

 

• Madras (Option 4): Associated with the Theosophical Society, whose headquarters is at Adyar.

question: Which stringed instrument is chiefly used by the Baul singers of Bengal to accompany their songs?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ektara.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Ektara is the instrument most closely associated with the Baul singers of Bengal. (एकतारा — बंगाल के बाउल गायक)

 

• As its name shows — *ek* meaning one and *tara* a string — it is a one-stringed instrument consisting of a gourd or wooden resonator with a bamboo neck. It is plucked with one finger and provides a drone against which the singer improvises.

 

• The Bauls are wandering minstrels of Bengal who belong to no organised sect and whose songs speak of the "man of the heart" (moner manush) and of a mystical devotion that ignores the distinctions of caste and creed. Lalon Fakir is their most celebrated figure, and Rabindranath Tagore was deeply influenced by their music.

 

• Baul songs were inscribed by UNESCO in 2005 as a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity. The Bauls also use the dotara, the khamak and the duggi.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Instruments and the traditions with which they are associated:
◦ Tambura (Tanpura) — the drone instrument of classical music, and held by the lead singer in Burrakatha and Pandavani
◦ Sarangi — the bowed instrument of Hindustani classical music
◦ Santoor — a hammered dulcimer of Kashmir; popularised by Pandit Shivkumar Sharma
◦ Rabab — an ancient plucked instrument of Afghan and Kashmiri origin
◦ Pung and Pena — Manipur; Dholak, Nagara, Shehnai — north India; Nadaswaram, Mridangam, Ghatam — Carnatic music

 

NOTE

 

• Sarangi (Option 2): A bowed instrument used to accompany khayal and thumri singing, not Baul music.

 

• Santoor (Option 3): A Kashmiri instrument played with light wooden mallets.

 

• Rabab (Option 4): Associated with Afghan music and with the early Sikh musical tradition of the rababis.

question: As per the Census of India, an urban agglomeration or city with a population of more than ten lakh is classified as a ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Million Plus City.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Census of India classifies an urban agglomeration or city with a population of more than ten lakh (one million) as a "Million Plus City", sometimes described as a metropolitan city. (दस लाख से अधिक जनसंख्या — मिलियन प्लस सिटी)

 

• Census 2011 recorded 53 Million Plus Urban Agglomerations/Cities in India, in which about 43% of the country's urban population lived. The three largest were Greater Mumbai, Delhi and Kolkata.

 

• A city with a population of over 50 lakh is termed a Mega City; there were three such in 2011 — Mumbai, Delhi and Kolkata.

 

• The Census classifies urban settlements by size into six classes:
◦ Class I — 1,00,000 and above
◦ Class II — 50,000 to 99,999
◦ Class III — 20,000 to 49,999
◦ Class IV — 10,000 to 19,999
◦ Class V — 5,000 to 9,999
◦ Class VI — below 5,000

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Census defines an urban area in two ways:
◦ Statutory Town — a place with a municipality, corporation, cantonment board or notified town area committee
◦ Census Town — a place satisfying three conditions: a population of at least 5,000; a density of at least 400 persons per sq km; and at least 75% of the male working population engaged in non-agricultural pursuits

 

• India's urban population in 2011 was 31.16%, up from 27.81% in 2001.

 

NOTE

 

• Class-I city (Option 1): Any city of 1 lakh and above, which includes but is far wider than the Million Plus category.

 

• Statutory town (Option 3) and Census town (Option 4): Categories defined by administrative status and by economic criteria respectively, not by the size of population alone.

question: India's first indigenously designed and built aircraft carrier, INS Vikrant, was constructed at which shipyard?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Cochin Shipyard.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• INS Vikrant, India's first indigenously designed and built aircraft carrier, was constructed at the Cochin Shipyard Limited at Kochi, Kerala, and was commissioned on 2 September 2022 by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. (आईएनएस विक्रांत — कोचीन शिपयार्ड)

 

• It was designed by the Directorate of Naval Design of the Indian Navy, has a displacement of about 45,000 tonnes, and carries around 30 aircraft including MiG-29K fighters and helicopters. It uses a STOBAR system — Short Take-Off But Arrested Recovery — with a ski-jump.

 

• India thus became one of a small group of nations — the United States, Russia, the United Kingdom, France and China — able to design and build an aircraft carrier.

 

• The name honours India's first aircraft carrier, the earlier INS Vikrant, acquired from Britain in 1961 and famous for its role in the 1971 war. The word *Vikrant* means courageous. The ship's motto is "Jayema Sam Yudhi Sprdhah".

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Major Indian defence shipyards and their work:
◦ Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders, Mumbai — destroyers and submarines, including the Kalvari-class (Scorpene) submarines
◦ Garden Reach Shipbuilders and Engineers, Kolkata — frigates and corvettes
◦ Hindustan Shipyard, Visakhapatnam — commercial vessels and submarine refits
◦ Goa Shipyard — patrol vessels for the Coast Guard

 

• India's other carrier is INS Vikramaditya, acquired from Russia in 2013. The Navy's nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarines are INS Arihant and INS Arighaat.

 

NOTE

 

• Mazagon Dock (Option 2): Builds India's submarines and principal destroyers, but not the carrier.

 

• Garden Reach (Option 3): Specialises in smaller warships and was the builder of India's first indigenous warship, INS Ajay.

 

• Hindustan Shipyard (Option 4): India's oldest shipyard, founded in 1941, but not the builder of INS Vikrant.

question: Which instrument is used to measure the humidity of the atmosphere?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Hygrometer.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A hygrometer is the instrument used to measure the humidity, that is, the amount of water vapour present in the atmosphere. (आर्द्रतामापी)

 

• Care must be taken not to confuse it with the hydrometer, which measures the relative density of liquids and works on the principle of flotation. The two names differ by a single letter but measure entirely different things.

 

• Related terms: absolute humidity is the actual mass of water vapour per unit volume of air, while relative humidity is the ratio of the vapour actually present to the maximum the air can hold at that temperature, expressed as a percentage. High relative humidity makes a hot day feel more oppressive, because sweat evaporates slowly.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Instruments and what they measure, frequently asked in SSC:
◦ Barometer — atmospheric pressure
◦ Anemometer — wind speed
◦ Lactometer — purity of milk
◦ Ammeter — electric current; Voltmeter — potential difference
◦ Seismograph — earthquake waves
◦ Manometer — pressure of a gas
◦ Odometer — distance travelled by a vehicle; Speedometer — its speed
◦ Sphygmomanometer — blood pressure
◦ Altimeter — altitude; Fathometer — depth of the ocean
◦ Pyrometer — very high temperatures
◦ Galvanometer — small electric currents

 

NOTE

 

• Hydrometer (Option 1): Measures the relative density or specific gravity of liquids; a lactometer is a form of hydrometer.

 

• Barometer (Option 2): Measures atmospheric pressure; a sudden fall in its reading indicates an approaching storm, and a steady rise fair weather.

 

• Anemometer (Option 4): Measures the speed of the wind.

question:
Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding the Gondwana coal deposits of India?

I. They account for the bulk of India's coal production.

II. The Damodar valley is a major Gondwana coalfield region.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both I and II.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both statements are correct. (गोंडवाना कोयला — भारत के उत्पादन का लगभग 98%, दामोदर घाटी प्रमुख क्षेत्र)

 

• Statement I is correct: the Gondwana coal deposits, formed about 250 million years ago, account for roughly 98% of India's total coal production. It is chiefly bituminous coal and is of good quality, though its ash content is relatively high.

 

• Statement II is correct: the Damodar valley, lying across Jharkhand and West Bengal, is the most important Gondwana coalfield region and contains Jharia, Raniganj, Bokaro, Giridih and Karanpura. Jharia is the largest coalfield of India and the principal source of coking coal.

 

• The other Gondwana coal-bearing river valleys are the Sone, Mahanadi, Godavari and Wardha valleys.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Tertiary coal, formed about 15 to 60 million years ago, is found in Assam, Meghalaya, Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland and Jammu & Kashmir. It has a low ash and high sulphur content and accounts for only a small share of production.

 

• Types of coal in ascending order of carbon content and quality: Peat → Lignite → Bituminous → Anthracite. Anthracite, the best variety, is found in India only in Jammu & Kashmir; lignite is mined chiefly at Neyveli in Tamil Nadu.

 

• The largest coal-producing states are Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Jharkhand. Coal India Limited, with headquarters at Kolkata, is the largest coal producer in the world. Coal mines were nationalised in 1973.

 

NOTE

 

• Options 1, 2 and 4 are incorrect, because both the given statements are factually accurate.

question: Who is the author of the novel 'The Namesake'?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Jhumpa Lahiri.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "The Namesake" (2003) was written by Jhumpa Lahiri. (द नेमसेक — झुम्पा लाहिड़ी)

 

• The novel follows the life of Gogol Ganguli, the son of Bengali immigrants in the United States, and deals with questions of identity, naming and belonging between two cultures. It was made into a film by Mira Nair in 2006.

 

• Jhumpa Lahiri won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 2000 for her first book, the short-story collection "Interpreter of Maladies". Her other works include "Unaccustomed Earth", "The Lowland" (shortlisted for the Booker Prize) and "In Other Words", a memoir written originally in Italian.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Well-known Indian and Indian-origin women writers in English:
◦ Kiran Desai — *The Inheritance of Loss*, Booker Prize 2006
◦ Arundhati Roy — *The God of Small Things*, Booker Prize 1997
◦ Anita Nair — *Ladies Coupe*, *Mistress*
◦ Chitra Banerjee Divakaruni — *The Palace of Illusions*, *Sister of My Heart*
◦ Anita Desai — *Clear Light of Day*, *In Custody*
◦ Shashi Deshpande — *That Long Silence*
◦ Geetanjali Shree — *Tomb of Sand*, International Booker Prize 2022

 

NOTE

 

• Kiran Desai (Option 2): Won the Booker Prize in 2006; she is the daughter of the novelist Anita Desai.

 

• Anita Nair (Option 3): Author of *Ladies Coupe* and *Mistress*.

 

• Chitra Banerjee Divakaruni (Option 4): Author of *The Palace of Illusions*, a retelling of the Mahabharata from Draupadi's point of view.

question: In the context of the LPG reforms of 1991, 'privatisation' primarily refers to ______.
option_1: the removal of quantitative restrictions on imports and exports
option_2: the transfer of ownership or management of public sector enterprises to the private sector
option_3: the integration of the Indian economy with the world economy
option_4: the abolition of the industrial licensing system
solution_text:
The correct answer is the transfer of ownership or management of public sector enterprises to the private sector.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Privatisation means the transfer of ownership, management or control of a public sector enterprise to the private sector. (निजीकरण)

 

• It may take several forms:
◦ Disinvestment — the sale of a part of the government's equity holding
◦ Strategic sale — the transfer of both ownership and management control, as in the sale of Air India to the Tata Group in 2022
◦ Franchising or contracting out of services

 

• The three elements of the 1991 New Economic Policy must be distinguished carefully:
◦ Liberalisation — the removal of unnecessary controls and restrictions on the domestic economy, such as the abolition of industrial licensing (retained for only a handful of industries), the end of the MRTP asset limit and the freeing of interest rates
◦ Privatisation — reducing the role of the public sector, as above
◦ Globalisation — integrating the Indian economy with the world economy, by reducing tariffs, removing quantitative restrictions and encouraging foreign investment

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The reforms were introduced under Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh, in response to a severe balance of payments crisis in which reserves had fallen to about two weeks of imports.

 

• The New Public Sector Enterprise Policy (2021) divides sectors into strategic, where a bare minimum of public enterprises is to be retained, and non-strategic, where enterprises are to be privatised or closed. DIPAM, under the Ministry of Finance, manages the process.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 describes an element of globalisation.

 

• Option 3 is the definition of globalisation itself.

 

• Option 4 describes liberalisation, and specifically the industrial policy reform of 1991.

question: Who is the author of the book 'The Palace of Illusions'?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Chitra Banerjee Divakaruni.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "The Palace of Illusions" (2008) was written by Chitra Banerjee Divakaruni. (द पैलेस ऑफ इल्यूजन्स — चित्रा बनर्जी दिवाकरुनी)

 

• It is a retelling of the Mahabharata from the point of view of Draupadi (Panchaali), and takes its title from the palace of Indraprastha built by Maya, in which illusion made water seem solid and solid ground seem water.

 

• Her other well-known works include "Sister of My Heart", "The Mistress of Spices", "One Amazing Thing", "The Forest of Enchantments" (the Ramayana told by Sita) and "The Last Queen" (on Rani Jindan).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Contemporary Indian mythological retellings frequently asked in SSC:
◦ Amish Tripathi — *The Immortals of Meluha*, *The Secret of the Nagas*, *The Oath of the Vayuputras* (Shiva Trilogy); *Ram: Scion of Ikshvaku*, *Sita: Warrior of Mithila*, *Raavan* (Ram Chandra Series)
◦ Ashwin Sanghi — *The Rozabal Line*, *Chanakya's Chant*, *The Krishna Key*, *The Vault of Vishnu*
◦ Anand Neelakantan — *Asura: Tale of the Vanquished*, *Ajaya*
◦ Devdutt Pattanaik — *Jaya*, *Sita*, *My Gita*

 

NOTE

 

• Anita Desai (Option 2): Author of *Clear Light of Day* and *In Custody*, thrice shortlisted for the Booker Prize.

 

• Arundhati Roy (Option 3): Author of *The God of Small Things*, Booker Prize 1997, and *The Ministry of Utmost Happiness*.

 

• Kiran Desai (Option 4): Author of *The Inheritance of Loss*, Booker Prize 2006.

question: The term 'Gutter' is primarily associated with which of the following sports?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bowling.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Gutter" is a term used in ten-pin bowling. It refers to the channel running along each side of the lane; a ball that rolls into it fails to strike any pin and the throw is called a gutter ball. (गटर — बॉलिंग)

 

• Other terms of bowling: Strike (all ten pins knocked down with the first ball), Spare (all ten down with two balls), Turkey (three consecutive strikes), Frame (one of the ten rounds of a game), Pin and Perfect game (a score of 300).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Terms associated with other sports, frequently asked in SSC:
◦ Golf — tee, birdie, bogey, eagle, putt, caddie, links, hole in one
◦ Archery — bull's eye, quiver, nock, fletching
◦ Squash — let, stroke, rally, tin, service box
◦ Football — shin guard, offside, corner kick, penalty, hat-trick
◦ Judo — Ippon, Waza-ari, Dojo, Tatami
◦ Chess — gambit, checkmate, stalemate, castling, en passant
◦ Tennis — deuce, love, ace, volley, smash, tie-breaker
◦ Billiards/Snooker — cue, break, pot, baulk, frame

 

NOTE

 

• Golf (Option 2): Uses tee, birdie and bogey; a golf course has 18 holes.

 

• Archery (Option 3): Uses bull's eye and quiver; the target has ten scoring rings.

 

• Squash (Option 4): Uses let and tin; the game is played in an enclosed court.

question: Which of the following forts is located in Madhya Pradesh?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Gwalior Fort.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Gwalior Fort is situated at Gwalior in Madhya Pradesh, on a steep sandstone hill. (ग्वालियर किला — मध्य प्रदेश)

 

• It is traditionally attributed to Raja Suraj Sen and was later held by the Tomaras, the Delhi Sultans, the Mughals, the Marathas and finally the Scindias. Babur described it as "the pearl among the fortresses of Hind".

 

• Its principal structures are the Man Mandir Palace, built by Raja Man Singh Tomar, the Gujari Mahal built for his queen Mrignayani and now an archaeological museum, the Teli ka Mandir and the Sas-Bahu Temples. The fort also contains one of the world's earliest recorded uses of the numeral zero, in an inscription of the ninth century.

 

• Tansen, one of the nine jewels of Akbar's court, was born near Gwalior, and the Tansen Samaroh music festival is held there every year.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Important forts of India and their states:
◦ Madhya Pradesh — Gwalior, Mandu, Orchha, Asirgarh
◦ Maharashtra — Sinhagad, Raigad, Pratapgad, Shivneri, Daulatabad, Sindhudurg
◦ Rajasthan — Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh, Amber, Jaisalmer, Ranthambore, Mehrangarh, Bharatpur (Lohagarh); the Hill Forts of Rajasthan are a UNESCO World Heritage Site
◦ Telangana — Golconda, Warangal
◦ Delhi — Red Fort, Purana Qila, Tughlaqabad
◦ West Bengal — Fort William; Tamil Nadu — Fort St. George

 

NOTE

 

• Sinhagad Fort (Option 2): Near Pune in Maharashtra, famous for the exploit of Tanaji Malusare in 1670.

 

• Chittorgarh Fort (Option 3): In Rajasthan, the largest fort in India and associated with Rani Padmini and Meera Bai.

 

• Golconda Fort (Option 4): In Telangana, the capital of the Qutb Shahi dynasty and once the centre of the diamond trade.

question: The Raisina Dialogue, India's flagship annual conference on geopolitics and geo-economics, is organised by the Ministry of External Affairs in partnership with which institution?
option_3: Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses
solution_text:
The correct answer is Observer Research Foundation.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Raisina Dialogue is organised jointly by the Ministry of External Affairs and the Observer Research Foundation (ORF), a New Delhi-based think tank. (रायसीना संवाद — विदेश मंत्रालय एवं ओआरएफ)

 

• It has been held annually at New Delhi since 2016, and takes its name from Raisina Hill, the seat of the Government of India. It is modelled on conferences such as the Shangri-La Dialogue of Singapore and the Munich Security Conference.

 

• It is a multilateral, multi-stakeholder conference at which heads of state, ministers, military officers, diplomats, journalists and scholars discuss questions of geopolitics, security, technology and economics.

 

• A chief guest of ministerial or head-of-government rank delivers the keynote address each year.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other important dialogues and forums associated with India:
◦ Shangri-La Dialogue — Singapore, on Asian security
◦ Munich Security Conference — Germany
◦ World Economic Forum — Davos, Switzerland
◦ Indian Ocean Conference — organised by the India Foundation
◦ Quad Leaders' Summit — India, USA, Japan and Australia
◦ Vibrant Gujarat and the Global Investors Summit — investment-focused

 

• India hosted the G20 Summit in September 2023 at New Delhi, under the theme "Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam — One Earth, One Family, One Future", at which the African Union was admitted as a permanent member.

 

NOTE

 

• Confederation of Indian Industry (Option 2): An industry association that organises business summits, but not the Raisina Dialogue.

 

• Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses (Option 3): Now the Manohar Parrikar IDSA, a defence think tank under the Ministry of Defence.

 

• Indian Council of World Affairs (Option 4): Housed at Sapru House, New Delhi, it conducts research in international affairs but is not the partner in this conference.

question: The first edition of the Khelo India Games was held in which year?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 2018.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The first edition of the Khelo India Games was held at New Delhi in January 2018, under the name Khelo India School Games. (खेलो इंडिया — प्रथम संस्करण 2018)

 

• From the second edition, held at Pune in 2019, the event was renamed the Khelo India Youth Games, and the age categories were widened to under-17 and under-21.

 

• The Khelo India Programme was launched by the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports in 2018, by merging three earlier schemes. Its objectives are to promote sport at the grassroots, to identify talent, and to build sporting infrastructure across the country. Selected athletes receive an annual scholarship for eight years.

 

• The programme now includes the Khelo India Youth Games, the Khelo India University Games (first held at Bhubaneswar in 2020), the Khelo India Winter Games (held in Ladakh and Jammu & Kashmir) and the Khelo India Para Games (first held in 2023).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Related schemes: the Target Olympic Podium Scheme (TOPS), launched in 2014 to support elite athletes preparing for the Olympics, and the Fit India Movement, launched on 29 August 2019.

 

• 29 August, the birth anniversary of Major Dhyan Chand, is observed as National Sports Day, on which the national sports awards are conferred.

 

• The Sports Authority of India (SAI) was set up in 1984, after the 1982 Asian Games at New Delhi.

 

NOTE

 

• 2016 (Option 1): The year of the Rio Olympics and of the launch of the Target Olympic Podium Scheme in its revised form, but not of the Khelo India Games.

 

• 2020 (Option 3): The year of the first Khelo India University Games, at Bhubaneswar.

 

• 2022 (Option 4): The year of the Khelo India Youth Games held in Haryana.

question: The ancient city of Hastinapur, closely associated with the Mahabharata, is located in which present-day state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Uttar Pradesh.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Hastinapur, the capital of the Kuru kingdom in the Mahabharata, is situated in the Meerut district of Uttar Pradesh, on the banks of the Ganga. (हस्तिनापुर — उत्तर प्रदेश)

 

• The Kuru Mahajanapada had Indraprastha and Hastinapur as its principal cities. Excavations at Hastinapur by B.B. Lal in the 1950s revealed Painted Grey Ware (PGW) pottery, associated with the later Vedic period, and evidence of the site having been abandoned after a flood — a detail that agrees with the Puranic tradition.

 

• Hastinapur is also an important Jain pilgrimage centre, being traditionally the birthplace of three Tirthankaras — Shantinatha, Kunthunatha and Aranatha.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Ancient cities and their modern locations, frequently asked:
◦ Indraprastha — Delhi
◦ Pataliputra / Kusumapura — Patna, Bihar
◦ Kashi — Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh
◦ Saket — Ayodhya, Uttar Pradesh
◦ Kanyakubja — Kannauj, Uttar Pradesh
◦ Ujjayini / Avantika — Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh
◦ Kaushambi — near Prayagraj; capital of the Vatsa Mahajanapada
◦ Takshashila — Taxila, in present-day Pakistan
◦ Vaishali — Bihar; capital of the Vajji confederacy

 

• The seven historic cities of Delhi are Lal Kot/Qila Rai Pithora, Siri, Tughlaqabad, Jahanpanah, Ferozabad, Dinpanah (Purana Qila) and Shahjahanabad.

 

NOTE

 

• Haryana (Option 2): The site of Kurukshetra, where the Mahabharata war was fought, and of Panipat, but not of Hastinapur.

 

• Punjab (Option 3) and Rajasthan (Option 4): Neither is associated with the Kuru capital.

question: The International Olympic Committee (IOC) was founded in 1894 by which of the following?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Pierre de Coubertin.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The International Olympic Committee (IOC) was founded on 23 June 1894 at the Sorbonne in Paris by Baron Pierre de Coubertin of France, who is called the "Father of the Modern Olympic Games". (पियरे डी कुबर्तिन — आधुनिक ओलंपिक के जनक)

 

• Its headquarters is at Lausanne, Switzerland, and 23 June is observed each year as Olympic Day.

 

• The first modern Olympic Games were held at Athens in 1896. The first President of the IOC was Demetrios Vikelas of Greece; Coubertin was its second President and held office from 1896 to 1925.

 

• The Olympic motto was "Citius, Altius, Fortius" — Faster, Higher, Stronger — to which "Communiter" (Together) was added in 2021. The Olympic rings, designed by Coubertin in 1913, represent the five inhabited continents.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The ancient Olympic Games were held at Olympia in Greece from 776 BCE, in honour of Zeus, and were abolished in 393 CE by the Roman emperor Theodosius I.

 

• The World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) was established in 1999, following the First World Conference on Doping in Sport convened by the IOC at Lausanne, Switzerland, in February that year. WADA's headquarters is at Montreal, Canada.

 

• The Indian Olympic Association was formed in 1927. India first participated as a nation in 1920 at Antwerp, and won its first hockey gold at Amsterdam in 1928.

 

NOTE

 

• Juan Antonio Samaranch (Option 2): President of the IOC from 1980 to 2001, under whom the Games became commercially successful.

 

• Thomas Bach (Option 3): A German lawyer and former Olympic fencing champion, President of the IOC from 2013.

 

• Avery Brundage (Option 4): The American who served as IOC President from 1952 to 1972.

question: Which allotrope of carbon is the hardest naturally occurring substance known?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Diamond.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Diamond is an allotrope of carbon and the hardest naturally occurring substance known, with a hardness of 10 on the Mohs scale. (हीरा — सबसे कठोर प्राकृतिक पदार्थ)

 

• The reason lies in its structure: each carbon atom is bonded to four others by strong covalent bonds in a rigid three-dimensional tetrahedral network. Because all four valence electrons are used in bonding, diamond has no free electrons and is therefore a bad conductor of electricity, though it is an excellent conductor of heat.

 

• Graphite, by contrast, has carbon atoms arranged in hexagonal layers held together by weak forces, so the layers slide over one another. This makes graphite soft and slippery, and since each carbon uses only three of its four valence electrons in bonding, the fourth is free and graphite is a good conductor of electricity — the only non-metal that is.

 

• Allotropy is the existence of an element in two or more forms in the same physical state. Carbon's crystalline allotropes are diamond, graphite and fullerene; its amorphous forms include coal, coke, charcoal, lampblack and animal charcoal.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Uses: diamond in cutting and drilling tools and in jewellery; graphite as a lubricant, in pencil leads, as electrodes and as a moderator in nuclear reactors; coke as a reducing agent in metallurgy; activated charcoal in gas masks and water filters.

 

• Fullerene (C-60), also called Buckminsterfullerene, has 60 carbon atoms arranged like a football and was discovered in 1985.

 

• Carbon is called the "king of elements" because of catenation, its ability to form long chains with itself, which gives rise to millions of organic compounds.

 

NOTE

 

• Graphite (Option 1): The softest common allotrope of carbon, and the only non-metal that conducts electricity well.

 

• Charcoal (Option 2): An amorphous form of carbon obtained by the destructive distillation of wood.

 

• Fullerene (Option 3): A crystalline allotrope discovered in 1985, but far softer than diamond.

question: Who was the first Indian to be awarded the Nobel Prize?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rabindranath Tagore.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Rabindranath Tagore was the first Indian — and the first Asian — to be awarded a Nobel Prize, receiving the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913 for his collection of poems "Gitanjali" (Song Offerings). (रवींद्रनाथ टैगोर — प्रथम भारतीय नोबेल पुरस्कार विजेता, 1913)

 

• He composed "Jana Gana Mana", the national anthem of India, and "Amar Sonar Bangla", the national anthem of Bangladesh. The national song of Sri Lanka was also inspired by his work.

 

• He founded Visva-Bharati at Santiniketan, was knighted in 1915, and renounced his knighthood in 1919 in protest against the Jallianwala Bagh massacre. He is popularly called "Gurudev".

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Indian and Indian-origin Nobel laureates:
◦ Rabindranath Tagore — Literature, 1913
◦ C.V. Raman — Physics, 1930, for the Raman Effect; the only Indian to win the science Nobel while working in India
◦ Har Gobind Khorana — Medicine, 1968 (US citizen)
◦ Mother Teresa — Peace, 1979
◦ Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar — Physics, 1983 (US citizen)
◦ Amartya Sen — Economics, 1998
◦ V.S. Naipaul — Literature, 2001
◦ Venkatraman Ramakrishnan — Chemistry, 2009
◦ Kailash Satyarthi — Peace, 2014, shared with Malala Yousafzai
◦ Abhijit Banerjee — Economics, 2019

 

• Marie Curie was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize (Physics, 1903) and the first person of any sex to win it twice (Chemistry, 1911).

 

NOTE

 

• C.V. Raman (Option 2): Won the Physics Nobel in 1930; 28 February is observed as National Science Day to mark the discovery of the Raman Effect.

 

• Mother Teresa (Option 3): Won the Peace Prize in 1979 and was canonised in 2016.

 

• Har Gobind Khorana (Option 4): Won the Medicine Prize in 1968 for work on the genetic code, as a naturalised citizen of the United States.
